title: The Bean House coffee shop
titleCn: 豆屋咖啡店商业案例研究

paragraphs.text: Section three.
You will hear two business students called Katie and Paul talking about a case study they're preparing on a coffee shop chain called The Bean House.
First, you have some time to look at questions twenty-one to twenty-five on page four.
Now listen carefully and answer questions twenty-one to twenty-five.
Okay, I think we've got everything.
Mm.
You know, it's not too late to choose something a bit more well-known for our case study, more international.

Well, I heard that investors in Saudi Arabia and Australia are showing an interest, so you never know how far it'll go. And next term, one of the papers is corporate responsibility and ethical behavior, and The Bean House is quite a good example of a business that believes in those things.
I think the other students would be quite keen to hear what we have to say.
Yeah, that's true.
Anyway, I spent ages writing the introduction. Did you get my email?

Uh, with the introduction in the attachment? Yes. I really like the style. I noticed, though, that you wrote that Andrew Reese was the one who thought of The Bean House and he was planning to run it himself.
Wasn't he?
Actually, it was John Reese, his brother, that came up with the concept, and he suggested to Andrew that they write up a business plan and see if a bank loan was possible.
I must have got that wrong.
Mm.
I'll do that bit again. Well, I remember when The Bean House cafes first started appearing in the city. They were really popular with the students.

Yes, but they've always been family-friendly too, and you get a lot of city workers going there. I think its point of difference, though, was that it was the first to use the fair trade range of coffee only, and none of the other chains were doing that.
I think that was a good move, yes. So customers knew that the people working on coffee plantations were being paid properly.
Mm.
I guess other chains are doing the same thing now.
Actually, I was thinking that for the presentation, we should bring in some of the products.
You mean get the other students to try them out? That'd be expensive for us.
Not if we persuaded a Bean House near to campus to donate them. It'd be good publicity for them.
Look, I don't want to pour cold water on your idea, but I really think we'd better stick to facts and figures and take a more serious approach to it.
Okay. Anyway, I'm happy to show all the PowerPoint material if you want to do the presentation.
Paul, you have to speak as well. That was in the criteria for the presentation. We can either split it or take turns for different sections.
All right. But let me go first so I can get it over and done with.
Before you hear the rest of the discussion, you have some time to look at questions twenty-six to thirty on page five.
Now listen and answer questions twenty-six to thirty.
So John and Andrew Reese tried to start a business in two thousand and five, did they?

That was the first attempt. The business plan was approved by the bank, and they'd actually found a vacant site right in the middle of the business district, an ideal spot for a cafe. But for one reason or another, their funds fell through, and they didn't have the capital they needed. So it was back to square one.

Right. So the venture was postponed for another two years to two thousand and seven, and that's when they opened the two original Bean Houses. There was one next to the university, right? And one next to the central train station.

Yes. There, I think. And their turnover, even in the first year, was huge. And John and Andrew decided the company could get bigger, but they didn't want to spend all their time running from cafe to cafe. So that's when they thought of turning into a franchise. And about two hundred and fifty applications in about two months were made by people all wanting to set up a Bean House. The problem was, though, the recession came, and people started cutting back on things like coffee.
That's why they introduced loyalty cards, wasn't it? As a way of keeping the customer base they'd already achieved.

Yes, but that was probably not as good a move as their next idea after the economic recovery. I think the free Wi-Fi really gave them the edge over their competitors, especially for city workers doing business in their lunch hours.
Yes, and students researching presentations.
We should probably mention the latest strategy. They just introduced a range of organic teas. I suppose they appeal to customers who don't like...
That is the end of section three. You now have half a minute to check your answers.
